The church has not been a pillar of structural change, nor has it served as a reliable engine of economic mobility or a catalyst for modern community development. Its influence is symbolic, not systemic, emotional, not infrastructural. In the Jim Crow South, white surveillance was even more intense. Pastors often had to negotiate with local white authorities, appease white politicians, and avoid any hint of political trouble to protect their members from retaliation. The notion that churches function as independent community centers is historically inaccurate. Their freedom was conditional and tightly constrained.
